name: Misner-Zapolsky Star of Infinite Central Density
description: A static sphere of fluid as stiff as light, $p = \rho c^2/3$, whose density is infinite at the centre and falls as $1/r^2$. Tolman and Oppenheimer and Volkoff found it in 1939, and it is the core that models of neutron stars approach as their central density grows without limit.
convention: We keep factors of $c$ and $G$ explicit, and the Ricci tensor is the standard contraction, $R_{\mu\nu} = R^\alpha{}_{\mu\alpha\nu}$.
history: A gas squeezed hard enough forgets what it is made of: its particles move so fast that their rest mass no longer counts, and the pressure climbs to a third of the energy density, $p = \rho c^2/3$, the ratio that holds for light [tolman1939]. J. Robert Oppenheimer and George Volkoff met that limit in 1939 at the centre of their star of cold neutrons, and followed it to a star whose central density has no bound [oppenheimer1939]. Their equations had one exact solution there: a mass $3c^2r/14G$ inside every radius $r$, and a density $3c^2/56\pi Gr^2$ [oppenheimer1939]. Richard Tolman reached the same sphere in the paper printed just before theirs, as a limit of the fifth and the sixth of his eight solutions, and suggested that it "might be called the blackbody radiation solution" [tolman1939].¶The sphere has no size of its own: at twice the radius it holds twice the mass, so $2Gm/c^2r = 3/7$ at every radius and $g_{rr} = 7/4$ throughout [oppenheimer1939]. Space at one moment is therefore a cone: a circle of circumference $2\pi r$ lies at a distance $\sqrt{7}\,r/2$ from the tip [tolman1939]. A clock at rest ticks at a rate proportional to $\sqrt{r}$ and stands still at the centre, where the density and the pressure are infinite, which Oppenheimer and Volkoff took for "the slowing down of all physical processes near the origin" [oppenheimer1939]. They checked that the infinite density hides no infinite number of neutrons: the count inside radius $r$ grows as $r^{3/2}$ [oppenheimer1939].¶A star needs a surface, and pure radiation has none: with $p = \rho c^2/3$ all the way out, the star would need an infinite radius [dev2002]. Tolman's fifth and sixth solutions put a surface on it [tolman1939]. Each has the sphere of radiation for its core and a pressure that drops to zero at a radius $r_b$, where Schwarzschild's vacuum takes over, around a mass of $c^2r_b/4G$ for the fifth and $3c^2r_b/14G$ for the sixth [tolman1939]. Oppenheimer and Volkoff carried the exact solution out to where their approximation gives way and integrated the rest numerically, which gave a star of 0.34 solar masses with a radius of 3.1 kilometers [oppenheimer1939]. Their heaviest star, at a finite central density, had 0.71 solar masses [oppenheimer1939]. They called the limit "a unique unstable singular solution" [oppenheimer1939].¶Is a star past the peak of the mass curve stable? Tolman had warned that a static solution alone cannot say whether its equilibrium "would be stable towards disturbances" [tolman1939]. The means to answer came in January 1964, with Subrahmanyan Chandrasekhar's equation for the radial pulsations of a star in general relativity [chandrasekhar1964prl]. Charles Misner and Harold Zapolsky, at the University of Maryland, solved it numerically in a letter printed that June, for models of neutron stars whose cores approach $p = \rho c^2/3$ at densities of $10^{15}$ grams per cubic centimeter and above [misner1964, chavanis2002]. The fundamental mode turns unstable at the star of greatest mass, and the denser stars beyond it are unstable too [misner1964, chavanis2002].¶Past its peak the mass oscillates about the mass of the singular sphere, less at each swing as the central density grows, and plotted against the radius the sequence of stars winds into a spiral with the singular sphere at its centre [chavanis2002, chavanis2008, meltzer1966]. The oscillation comes from the way a star of finite central density settles onto the singular one: far from its centre its density overshoots $3c^2/56\pi Gr^2$ and then undershoots it, by a fraction that goes as $r^{-3/4}\cos\left(\tfrac{\sqrt{47}}{4}\ln r + \delta\right)$ with $\delta$ a constant [chavanis2002]. Misner and Zapolsky could follow only the fundamental mode [chavanis2002]. Pierre-Henri Chavanis settled the rest in 2002 for spheres of this fluid held in a box, where every further peak and trough of the mass hands one more mode of pulsation to instability [chavanis2002].¶The same metric describes a ball of light with no neutrons in it: Rafael Sorkin, Robert Wald, and Zhang Zhen Jiu shut thermal radiation in a spherical box in 1981 and looked for the arrangement with the most entropy [sorkin1981]. The extrema of the entropy are the static solutions, and the stable ones are its local maxima [sorkin1981]. A box of radius $R$ holds at most a mass of $0.493\,c^2R/2G$, more than the $3c^2R/14G$ of the singular sphere, toward which the mass oscillates as the centre grows hotter [chavanis2008]. Krsna Dev and Marcelo Gleiser took another way to a surface in 2002: they kept a density that falls as $1/r^2$ and let the pressure along the radius differ from the pressure across it, which closes the sphere at a finite radius [dev2002].

related.text: The equations of equilibrium for a star with any equation of state. Fed $p = \rho c^2/3$ and an infinite central density they have one solution, $m = 3c^2r/14G$, which Oppenheimer and Volkoff wrote down in the paper that introduced them [oppenheimer1939].

The seventh of Richard Tolman's eight solutions, a star whose density falls as $1 - r^2/R^2$ from a finite value at the centre. The stars here are his fifth and sixth, which he built for an infinite one [tolman1939].

The star of uniform density, solution III on Tolman's list. Its central pressure is infinite only at $R = \frac{9}{8}r_s$, while the density of this star is infinite at the centre whatever its size [tolman1939, schwarzschild1916b, buchdahl1959].
The vacuum outside the star. Tolman's fifth and sixth solutions meet it where their pressure vanishes, at $r_b = 2r_s$ for the fifth and $r_b = \frac{7}{3}r_s$ for the sixth [tolman1939].

The collapse this star points to. Oppenheimer and Volkoff ended their paper on stars too heavy for any equilibrium, whose nonstatic solutions were "now being investigated", and Oppenheimer and Hartland Snyder followed one through later that year [oppenheimer1939, oppenheimersnyder1939].
A star of uniform density with unequal pressures, from 1974. Krsna Dev and Marcelo Gleiser took it up in 2002 before they gave the $1/r^2$ sphere unequal pressures of its own [bowers1974, dev2002].

coordinates.name: Blackbody Radiation Solution

parameters.description: Any length; it fixes the rate of $t$, the proper time of a clock at rest at $r = a$. Whatever its value, the density is $\rho = 3c^2/(56\pi Gr^2)$, the pressure $p = \rho c^2/3$, and the mass inside radius $r$ is $m = 3c^2r/(14G)$

coordinates.convention: We use the limit that Tolman's solutions V and VI share with Oppenheimer and Volkoff's exact solution, in coordinates $(t, r, \theta, \phi)$, with $t$ carrying dimensions of time and $r$ the areal radius. The length $a$ is free, and $t$ is the proper time of a clock at rest at $r = a$. We take components in the chart $x^0 = ct$, and a dot in the geodesic equations is a derivative with respect to an affine parameter, so $\dot{t}$ means $d(ct)/d\lambda$.

coordinates.name: Tolman V Star

parameters.description: Radius of the star, where the pressure vanishes and Schwarzschild's vacuum begins, around the mass $M = c^2r_b/(4G)$; Tolman's constant of solution V is $R = 14^{3/7}r_b$
The component $g^{rr} = 1 - 2Gm(r)/(c^2r)$, with $m(r)$ the mass inside radius $r$; it is $4/7$ at the centre and $1/2$ at the surface, and $\partial_rZ = (7Z - 4)/(3r)$

coordinates.convention: We use Tolman's solution V at his exponent $n = 1/2$, joined to Schwarzschild's vacuum, in coordinates $(t, r, \theta, \phi)$, with $t$ carrying dimensions of time and $r$ the areal radius. The star has radius $r_b$, and $t$ is the proper time of a clock at rest far from it. We write $Z$ for $g^{rr}$. We take components in the chart $x^0 = ct$, and a dot in the geodesic equations is a derivative with respect to an affine parameter, so $\dot{t}$ means $d(ct)/d\lambda$.

coordinates.name: Tolman VI Star

parameters.description: Radius of the star, where the pressure vanishes and Schwarzschild's vacuum begins, around the mass $M = 3c^2r_b/(14G)$; Tolman's constants of solution VI are $A = 9/\sqrt{112\,r_b}$ and $B = A/(9r_b)$

coordinates.convention: We use Tolman's solution VI at his exponent $n = 1/2$, joined to Schwarzschild's vacuum, in coordinates $(t, r, \theta, \phi)$, with $t$ carrying dimensions of time and $r$ the areal radius. The star has radius $r_b$, and $t$ is the proper time of a clock at rest far from it. We take components in the chart $x^0 = ct$, and a dot in the geodesic equations is a derivative with respect to an affine parameter, so $\dot{t}$ means $d(ct)/d\lambda$.

coordinates.name: Tolman's Exponent

parameters.description: Tolman's exponent in solution V, a pure number with $0 < n \le 1$. The pressure is $p = n\rho c^2/(2 - n)$ and the density $\rho = n(2 - n)c^2/(8\pi G(1 + 2n - n^2)r^2)$: $n = 1/2$ is radiation, and at $n = 1$ sound travels at the speed of light
Any length; it fixes the rate of $t$, the proper time of a clock at rest at $r = a$

coordinates.convention: We use Tolman's solution V with his exponent $n$ free and his constant $R \to \infty$, in coordinates $(t, r, \theta, \phi)$, with $t$ carrying dimensions of time and $r$ the areal radius. The length $a$ is free, and $t$ is the proper time of a clock at rest at $r = a$. We take components in the chart $x^0 = ct$, and a dot in the geodesic equations is a derivative with respect to an affine parameter, so $\dot{t}$ means $d(ct)/d\lambda$.
